title: Media literacy & misinformation
examples: How do I know if this news story is true?
What is the difference between bias and truth?
Can you show me an example of a deepfake?

explain.say: Today we are learning about media literacy skills. This means knowing how to use and understand media. We will learn to spot false information online.
First we must learn about checking sources carefully. Always ask where the information first came from. A good source is reliable and trustworthy.

draw.text: Checking Sources: Where did it come from?

explain.say: Next we need to look for bias in the reporting. Bias means showing favouritism toward one side. Always look for different viewpoints.

draw.text: Bias: Showing favouritism to one side

explain.say: Our third topic is understanding deepfakes. These are fake videos or audio using AI. They make it look like someone said something they did not.
For a real-life example think about advertisements. Sometimes ads show things that are not true. You must check if the product claims are backed up by facts.
The most common mistake is accepting everything you see online. Always pause and think before you share any shocking information. Take a moment to verify your sources first.

faq.q: How do I know if a website is trustworthy?
faq.a: Look for the website's 'about us' page to see who runs it. Also, check if they cite their sources for big claims. You might also ask if the website has a clear contact page.
asks: Is it okay to trust random websites?
How can I check a website's credibility?

faq.q: What is the difference between opinion and fact?
faq.a: A fact can be proven true with evidence, like a date or a measurement. An opinion is a belief or feeling that someone has. You might ask if the statement can be proven true.
asks: How do I tell if something is just someone's view?

faq.q: Are deepfakes always used for bad things?
faq.a: Deepfakes can be used to trick people or spread lies. However, they can also be used in education or art for fun. You should always question the source.
asks: Can deepfakes be used for good?
What is the danger of fake videos?

faq.q: If two sources disagree, which one should I believe?
faq.a: It is best to find a third, highly reputable source that covers the topic. Comparing multiple sources helps you see the full picture. You can ask if major news organizations agree.
asks: How do I handle conflicting reports?
Should I trust the first source I see?

faq.a: This is when you only look for information that already agrees with what you believe. To fight this, you must actively seek out viewpoints you disagree with. You can ask a friend with different views.
asks: Why do I only believe things I agree with?
What is the trap of only reading one side?

facts: Misinformation is false information shared without knowing it is false.
Bias is a preference or prejudice toward a particular person or idea.
Deepfakes use artificial intelligence to manipulate media content.
Checking sources means finding the original evidence for a claim.

quiz.say: A news article strongly criticizes one political party but never mentions any positive things about them. This is an example of:
quiz.why: The article only shows one side, which is the definition of bias.

wrong.0: Source checking is the action you take, not the type of bias shown in the article.
wrong.2: Misinformation means the facts themselves are untrue, but the article might be factually correct, just unfair.
wrong.3: A deepfake is a manipulated video or audio, not just slanted writing.

quiz.say: If you see a video of a celebrity saying something shocking, but you know the video might be edited, what is the best first step?

options.show: Search for confirmation from multiple reputable news outlets.
options.say: Search for confirmation from multiple reputable news outlets.

options.show: Share it quickly to warn others.
options.say: Share it quickly to warn others.

quiz.why: Relying on multiple established sources is the best way to verify digital media.

wrong.0: Comments sections can be filled with other misinformation and opinions.
wrong.2: Sharing quickly spreads the fake information before you can check it.
wrong.3: Assuming it is true is the biggest mistake when dealing with unverified media.

quiz.say: A website claims a new medicine cures everything, but it provides no scientific studies or names of researchers. This claim is most likely:
quiz.why: A key part of media literacy is demanding proof, not just strong claims.

wrong.1: A deepfake is media manipulation, not necessarily a medical claim.
wrong.2: Neutral reporting requires presenting evidence from various sides.
wrong.3: While it is an opinion, the lack of evidence makes it more than just a simple opinion.
